F1.quote: Producing the information needed to address risks from AI … Authoritative data and frameworks to help you identify, prioritize, and manage the risks from AI

F2.locus: Our tools and data: 'What are the risks from AI?'

F3.quote: A living database of 1,700+ AI risks from 65 frameworks
F3.claim: the home page's count: 1,700+ risks from 65 frameworks

F4.locus: blog: 'Explore the Frameworks Behind the AI Risk Repository'
F4.quote: This post shares a public Google Slides deck containing all 65 frameworks included in Version 3 of the AI Risk Repository. It provides direct access to source documents, diagrams, and key excerpts to support transparency, research, and further analysis of AI risk classifications.
F4.claim: the 65 Version 3 frameworks published as a deck with source documents, diagrams and key excerpts
F4.lineage: the unit and its evidence: a risk as a framework states it

F5.quote: Data from the MIT AI Risk Initiative is licensed under CC BY 4.0
F5.claim: the Initiative's data licensed CC BY 4.0
F5.lineage: openness: free to copy, CC BY 4.0

F6.quote: Integration of 22 new AI risk frameworks, bringing the total number of included documents to 65. … Expansion of the AI Risk Database to 1,612 unique risk entries, each systematically extracted and coded.
F6.claim: the April 2025 update: 22 new frameworks to 65 documents, 1,612 unique risk entries

F7.quote: Introduction of a new risk subdomain on multi-agent risks, reflecting recent developments in AI research on complex agent interactions.
F7.claim: a new subdomain on multi-agent risks
F7.lineage: the Domain Taxonomy: seven domains and their subdomains

F8.quote: A Domain Taxonomy, which classifies risks into seven thematic domains and 25 more granular subdomains.
F8.claim: the domain taxonomy given as seven domains and 25 subdomains (other own pages give 24)
F8.lineage: the Domain Taxonomy: seven domains and their subdomains

F9.quote: The AI Risk Repository is a structured and evolving resource that aims to consolidate and clarify how risks from artificial intelligence are categorized across academic, industry, and policy literatures.
F9.claim: a structured, evolving resource consolidating how AI risks are categorized across literatures
F9.lineage: what it is: a living database of AI risks from frameworks

F10.quote: Updated Version of the AI Risk Repository Preprint Now Available … Original release: August 2024 … Updated version: April 2025
F10.claim: the preprint's versions: August 2024 original, April 2025 update
F10.lineage: the paper: Slattery et al., arXiv:2408.12622, Patterns 2026

F11.quote: A new MIT FutureTech project reviewed 43 AI frameworks produced by research, industry and government organizations; they identified 777 risks in total.
F11.claim: the first release: an MIT FutureTech project, 43 frameworks, 777 risks

F12.quote: The repository includes a risk database linking each risk to the source information (paper title, authors) and supporting evidence, such as quotes and page numbers.
F12.claim: each risk linked to its source and supporting evidence (quotes, page numbers)
F12.lineage: the unit and its evidence: a risk as a framework states it

F13.quote: The key finding from our analysis is that there are significant gaps in existing risk frameworks, with the average framework covering only 34% of the identified risk subdomains and even the most significant frameworks covering only 70%.
F13.claim: Slattery: the average framework covers 34% of subdomains, the most comprehensive 70%
F13.lineage: headline findings: coverage gaps and causes

F14.quote: most of the risks (51%) were caused by AI systems rather than humans (34%), and were found after the AI model was trained and deployed (65%) rather than before (10%).
F14.claim: the first release's causal figures: AI 51%, human 34%; post-deployment 65%, pre-deployment 10%
F14.lineage: headline findings: coverage gaps and causes

F15.quote: We expect that what we have produced will need some modification before it is useful for most audiences, but we hope that it provides a solid foundation.
F15.claim: Slattery: it will need modification before it is useful for most audiences

F16.quote: In less than a week, over 35,000 people have used the website and over 6,000 have viewed our explainer video on YouTube.
F16.claim: first week: over 35,000 website users, over 6,000 views of the explainer

F17.quote: This comprises a living database of 777 risks extracted from 43 taxonomies, which can be filtered based on two overarching taxonomies and easily accessed, modified, and updated via our website and online spreadsheets.
F17.claim: v1: a living database of 777 risks from 43 taxonomies, filtered by two taxonomies, via website and spreadsheets

F18.quote: We construct our Repository with a systematic review of taxonomies and other structured classifications of AI risk followed by an expert consultation. We develop our taxonomies of AI risk using a best-fit framework synthesis.
F18.claim: method: systematic review, then expert consultation; taxonomies by best-fit framework synthesis
F18.lineage: method: systematic review, expert consultation, best-fit synthesis

F19.quote: Our high-level Causal Taxonomy of AI Risks classifies each risk by its causal factors (1) Entity: Human, AI; (2) Intentionality: Intentional, Unintentional; and (3) Timing: Pre-deployment; Post-deployment.
F19.claim: the Causal Taxonomy: entity, intentionality, timing
F19.lineage: the Causal Taxonomy: entity, intent, timing

F20.quote: Our mid-level Domain Taxonomy of AI Risks classifies risks into seven AI risk domains: (1) Discrimination & toxicity, (2) Privacy & security, (3) Misinformation, (4) Malicious actors & misuse, (5) Human-computer interaction, (6) Socioeconomic & environmental, and (7) AI system safety, failures, & limitations. These are further divided into 23 subdomains.
F20.claim: the Domain Taxonomy: seven domains named, 23 subdomains (v1)
F20.lineage: the Domain Taxonomy: seven domains and their subdomains

F21.quote: The AI Risk Repository is, to our knowledge, the first attempt to rigorously curate, analyze, and extract AI risk frameworks into a publicly accessible, comprehensive, extensible, and categorized risk database.
F21.claim: to its authors' knowledge the first such curated, extracted, categorized risk database
F21.lineage: purpose: a common frame of reference for AI risk

F22.quote: The Navigator connects MIT's AI Risk Repository datasets through a shared taxonomy, so you can move between them and surface the patterns that matter.

F23.quote: This is a research prototype. The data and analyses are preliminary and not yet validated

F50.claim: limits: clarity over nuance; no impact, likelihood or interaction

F51.claim: the database free to copy and use

F53.quote: Because these classification systems were so different, it was hard to unify them; high-level risk categories such as “Diffusion of responsibility” or “Humans create dangerous AI by mistake” do not map to narrower categories like “Misuse” or “Noisy Training Data,” or vice versa.
F53.claim: why two taxonomies: causal categories and hazard categories do not map onto each other

F55.quote: Use this file to orient LLMs and AI agents to the main AIRI resources at airisk.mit.edu and the related AI Risk Navigator.
F55.claim: a file addressed to LLMs and AI agents, orienting them to the Initiative's resources

F56.quote: Refer to the project as the MIT AI Risk Initiative, or AIRI when the abbreviation is useful. … Treat AIRI resources as living datasets. Check the linked pages before giving exact counts, dates, version numbers, or coverage claims.

F57.quote: Do not present AIRI datasets as legal, safety, or investment advice. They are research resources and decision-support tools.

F58.quote: For questions about observed harms, use the MIT AI Incident Tracker and distinguish reported incidents from predicted risks. … For cross-dataset questions, use the MIT AI Risk Navigator, but note that it is a research prototype and may contain preliminary analyses.
